# Introduction

`r Biocpkg("ModuleViz")` clusters feature trajectories from longitudinal omics
experiments and renders ordered temporal heatmaps.

The workflow is useful for RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN, or other
feature-by-sample matrices where columns represent ordered time points,
treatment conditions, or both.

This vignette uses the small bundled `heatmap_example` dataset so the tutorial
runs without network access.

# Load The Example Time-Course

```{r load}
library(ModuleViz)
data("heatmap_example")

mat <- heatmap_example$mat
meta <- heatmap_example$meta

dim(mat)
head(meta)
```

The returned object is plain R data:

- `mat`: numeric feature-by-sample matrix.
- `meta`: one row per sample, with sample ID, condition, time, and replicate.

# Choose The Number Of Modules

`choose_k()` calculates a simple within-cluster-sum-of-squares elbow diagnostic.
Use it as a first pass, then choose a biologically interpretable value.

```{r choose-k}
diag <- choose_k(
  zscore_rows(mat),
  k_range = 2:5,
  method = "kmeans"
)

diag
attr(diag, "suggested_k")
```

# Cluster Temporal Patterns

```{r cluster}
obj <- longitudinal_cluster(
  mat,
  meta,
  sample_col = "SampleID",
  time_col = "TimeHr",
  group_col = "Condition",
  k = 4,
  method = "kmeans",
  aggregate_replicates = TRUE,
  stability = TRUE,
  n_resample = 10
)

obj
```

Clusters are reordered by their temporal peak, so early-high modules appear
before late-high modules.

# Draw The Heatmap

```{r heatmap, fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
longitudinal_heatmap(
  obj,
  annotation_cols = c("Condition", "TimeHr"),
  top_n_label = 3,
  cluster_palette = "spectral"
)
```

To save a PDF:

```{r save-heatmap}
longitudinal_heatmap(
  obj,
  annotation_cols = c("Condition", "TimeHr"),
  top_n_label = 3,
  file = file.path(tempdir(), "example_heatmap.pdf"),
  width = 5,
  height = 6.5
)
```

# Plot Module Trajectories

```{r lineplot, fig.width=4.3, fig.height=4.3}
pattern_lineplot(obj, palette = "nature")
```

# Draw Side-By-Side RNA And ATAC Patterns

`dual_heatmap()` is the two-layer case of `multi_heatmap()` (next section).

The primary matrix drives clustering and row order. The secondary matrix is
aligned by gene and displayed next to it. This example simulates two ATAC peaks
per gene using the bundled expression data so the code is fully runnable.

```{r dual-omics, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=5}
set.seed(99)
genes <- rownames(mat)
atac <- mat[rep(seq_along(genes), each = 2), , drop = FALSE]
rownames(atac) <- paste0(
  "Peak",
  sprintf("%03d", seq_len(nrow(atac))),
  "_",
  rep(genes, each = 2)
)
atac <- atac + matrix(rnorm(length(atac), sd = 0.35), nrow = nrow(atac))

dual_heatmap(
  primary = obj,
  secondary = atac,
  primary_name = "RNA",
  secondary_name = "ATAC",
  gene_of_primary = function(id) id,
  gene_of_secondary = function(id) sub("^.*_", "", id),
  aggregate = "mean",
  label_features = c("Gene001", "Gene016", "Gene031", "Gene046"),
  cluster_palette = "spectral"
)
```

# Draw Several Data Types Together

`multi_heatmap()` takes a named list of any number of layers (here RNA, ATAC,
H3K27ac, and H3K27me3) and draws one panel per layer. Every panel shares the RNA
module split and row order, and one z-score legend covers all of them. Each
layer is z-scored within itself and collapsed to one row per gene, so peaks and
genes line up row for row.

The two histone layers are simulated: an activating mark that follows
expression and a repressive mark that mirrors it.

```{r multi-heatmap, fig.width=9.3, fig.height=5.6}
as_regions <- function(m, sign = 1, sd = 0.5) {
  out <- sign * m + matrix(rnorm(length(m), sd = sd), nrow = nrow(m))
  rownames(out) <- paste0("region", seq_len(nrow(m)), "_", rownames(m))
  out
}
layers <- list(
  RNA      = obj,
  ATAC     = atac,
  H3K27ac  = as_regions(mat),
  H3K27me3 = as_regions(mat, sign = -1)
)

multi <- multi_heatmap(
  layers,
  meta = meta, sample_col = "SampleID", time_col = "TimeHr",
  group_col = "Condition",
  label_features = c("Gene001", "Gene016", "Gene031", "Gene046"),
  cluster_palette = "spectral",
  show_column_names = FALSE
)
multi
```

`multi_lineplot()` draws each module's mean trajectory in every layer, which
shows at a glance which marks follow expression and which oppose it. Modules
are stacked in one column by default; `split_groups = TRUE` gives each
condition its own column and `ncol` wraps the modules into a grid.

```{r multi-lineplot, fig.width=5.6, fig.height=5}
multi_lineplot(multi, split_groups = TRUE)
```

To cluster on all layers together instead of on RNA alone, use
`cluster_by = "joint"`. `gene_set = "reference"` keeps every RNA gene and draws
layers without that gene in grey.

```{r multi-joint, fig.width=9.3, fig.height=5.6}
multi_heatmap(
  layers,
  meta = meta, sample_col = "SampleID", time_col = "TimeHr",
  group_col = "Condition", cluster_by = "joint", k = 4,
  cluster_palette = "spectral", show_column_names = FALSE
)
```

# Module Enrichment

`module_enrichment()` tests each module against gene sets you supply (a named
list, a two-column data frame, or a GMT file). Passing the result to the
heatmap prints the top terms beside each module.

```{r enrichment, fig.width=5.9, fig.height=5}
genes <- rownames(mat)
gene_sets <- list(
  Early_response = genes[1:15],
  Mid_response = genes[16:30],
  Late_response = genes[31:45],
  Housekeeping = genes[seq(2, 60, by = 4)]
)
enr <- module_enrichment(obj, gene_sets, min_size = 3)
head(enr[, 1:9])

longitudinal_heatmap(obj, enrichment = enr, top_n_label = 2)
```

# Single-Cell Pseudobulk Example

Single-cell data are summarized into pseudobulk profiles by sample, cell type,
condition, and time point with `pseudobulk_cells()`, which accepts a
`SingleCellExperiment`, a `Seurat` object, or a count matrix with per-cell
metadata. The result is a `SummarizedExperiment` that
`longitudinal_cluster()` takes directly.

```{r single-cell-pseudobulk, fig.width=4.3, fig.height=4.3}
sce <- simulate_single_cell_example(cells_per_sample = 15,
                                    cell_types = c("T_cell", "Monocyte",
                                                   "B_cell"))
sce

pb <- pseudobulk_cells(
  sce,
  time_col = "TimeHr",
  sample_col = "SampleID",
  group_col = "Condition",
  celltype_col = "CellType"
)
pb$Group <- paste(pb$CellType, pb$Condition, sep = "_")

sc_obj <- longitudinal_cluster(
  pb,
  time_col = "TimeHr",
  group_col = "Group",
  k = 4,
  aggregate_replicates = TRUE,
  stability = FALSE
)

pattern_lineplot(sc_obj, palette = "science")
```

# Export Tables

```{r write}
out_dir <- tempdir()
write_memberships(obj, prefix = file.path(out_dir, "heatmap_example"))
```

This writes:

- `heatmap_example_memberships.txt`
- `heatmap_example_centroids.txt`
- `heatmap_example_stability.txt`

# Real Public Data

The package also includes a helper for public datasets in Bioconductor
`timecoursedata`. These examples are optional because they require installing
the experiment-data package.

```{r available}
available_real_timecourse_datasets()
```

Install the optional data package before running the real-data workflow:

```{r install-timecoursedata, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("timecoursedata")
```

```{r sorghum, eval=requireNamespace("timecoursedata", quietly = TRUE)}
sorghum <- load_real_timecourse_example(
  dataset = "sorghum_leaf",
  genotype = "BT642",
  min_week = 3,
  top_n_features = 1000
)
```

For the mouse influenza microarray dataset:

```{r influenza, eval=requireNamespace("timecoursedata", quietly = TRUE)}
flu <- load_real_timecourse_example(
  dataset = "influenza_mouse",
  group = c("C", "K", "M"),
  top_n_features = 1000
)
```
